borders.before: the lecturer's self-introduction, practical course links, and the specific learning outcomes for the lecture
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary, and microenvironmental disease
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing that sets course expectations, while Subtopic 2 begins substantive scientific instruction on what cancer is.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 3 would mistakenly pull foundational biological definitions into the introductory framing.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would conflate introductory framing and course logistics with the fundamental biological definition of malignancy.

borders.before: the public interpretation of intrinsic 'bad luck' versus environmental cancer risk and global epidemiological variations
borders.after: infectious agents, chronic inflammation from pathogens, and viral oncogenesis mechanisms
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 concludes the high-level overview of global epidemiology, whereas Subtopic 7 begins the detailed examination of specific carcinogen categories starting with infectious agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 6 would detach the discussion of geographic variations from the broader etiologic framework in subtopic 5, while moving to subtopic 8 would isolate Burkitt lymphoma from the survey of infectious agents.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would merge general epidemiological concepts with specific microbiological mechanisms of carcinogenesis.

borders.before: the historical discovery, geographic distribution, and translocation mechanism of Epstein-Barr virus in Burkitt lymphoma
borders.after: dietary mutagens such as aflatoxin, hepatic cytochrome oxidase activation, and DNA adduct formation
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 8 concludes the topic on pathogen-induced oncogenesis, while Subtopic 9 initiates the topic on chemical and physical DNA-damaging agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 8 would group a viral lymphoma case study with chemical mutagens, while moving to subtopic 10 would separate aflatoxin from other chemical carcinogens.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would blur the distinction between pathogen-driven malignant transformation and the biochemical mechanisms of direct chemical mutagenesis.

borders.before: beta-naphthylamine metabolism and the tissue-specific activation of aromatic amines in the bladder
borders.after: asbestos, chronic inflammation, and the distinction between non-mutagenic promoters and direct mutagens
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 13 finishes the discussion of direct/xenobiotic chemical mutagens, whereas Subtopic 14 introduces the non-mutagenic mechanism of chronic inflammation and tumour promotion.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving to subtopic 13 would place bladder-specific chemical mutagens with non-mutagenic promoters, while moving to subtopic 15 would separate the asbestos case study from the initiator/promoter concepts it exemplifies.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would overlook the fundamental conceptual shift from direct DNA-damaging initiators to non-mutagenic promotional microenvironments.

borders.before: a synthesis summarizing direct mutagens, xenobiotic metabolism, promoters, and host developmental susceptibility
borders.after: mutational signature analysis and whole-genome sequencing methods used to identify carcinogen exposure
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 concludes the substantive biological causes of cancer with a summary, whereas Subtopic 18 begins a new section on experimental and analytical methodologies for proving carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving to subtopic 17 would pull the summary slide into the methodology topic, while moving to subtopic 19 would separate genomic sequencing signatures from epidemiological proof methods.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would combine the biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis with the experimental and computational toolsets used to prove them.

borders.before: the Ames test, S9 liver extract metabolic activation, and the limitations of in vitro carcinogenicity testing
borders.after: risk-benefit evaluations of carcinogen exposure, overall lecture takeaways, and closing remarks
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 completes the review of experimental methodologies, while Subtopic 22 provides the lecture's final conclusion and societal framing.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 21 would improperly include specific in vitro laboratory protocols within the closing topic.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would mix technical toxicology assay details with closing remarks and high-level risk-benefit conclusions.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2–4 discuss the biological definitions of cancer and specific mutagenic exposures, while Subtopics 5–6 address the public understanding of the 'bad luck' debate and global epidemiological data.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 collectively establish the overarching conceptual framework of cancer etiology, weighing intrinsic genetic processes against environmental exposures and population-level evidence before diving into specific carcinogen classes.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 surveys a variety of bacterial, fungal, and viral pathogens, whereas Subtopic 8 is an in-depth case study of Denis Burkitt's discovery and the molecular etiology of Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 serves as the primary mechanistic case study directly illustrating the principles of infectious oncogenesis introduced in Subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9–10 cover dietary fungal toxins and UV radiation, whereas Subtopics 11–13 focus specifically on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and xenobiotic metabolism via the AhR/CYP1A1 pathway.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 9 through 13 form a cohesive, continuous walkthrough of physical and chemical mutagens, explaining how they undergo metabolic activation to induce DNA adducts, dimers, and base transversions.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14–15 establish the initiator versus promoter paradigm through asbestos and the Berenbaum model, whereas Subtopics 16–17 explore host developmental susceptibility and provide a summary of mechanisms.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14 through 17 together cover non-mutagenic aspects of carcinogenesis—including microenvironmental inflammation, tumour promotion pathways, and host developmental timing—concluding with an integrated summary.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18–19 focus on human genomic signatures and population biobanks, while Subtopics 20–21 address laboratory toxicology using animal models and bacterial Ames tests.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 systematically address a single core question—how carcinogenicity is determined—by surveying genomic, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro methodologies.

topics.label: Course Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: It provides opening framing by introducing the lecturer, the cancer lecture series, and the key learning outcomes.

topics.label: Conceptual Foundations of Cancer Etiology and Risk
topics.groupedBecause: It explores the fundamental definition of cancer as a multi-step genetic disease influenced by intrinsic cellular errors, environmental mutagens, and epidemiological variations.

topics.label: Pathogen-Driven Carcinogenesis and Burkitt Lymphoma
topics.groupedBecause: It examines how infectious agents drive malignancy, detailed through the epidemiological and molecular mechanism of Epstein-Barr virus in Burkitt lymphoma.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Chemical and Physical Mutagenesis
topics.groupedBecause: It details how dietary toxins, UV radiation, and xenobiotically metabolized chemical compounds induce DNA adducts, dimers, and base transversions.

topics.label: Tumour Promotion, Inflammation, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: It investigates non-mutagenic factors in carcinogenesis, including chronic inflammation, the initiator/promoter paradigm, host developmental susceptibility, and synthesizes these biological mechanisms.

topics.label: Methodologies for Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: It surveys the analytical, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro experimental techniques used to determine whether an agent is carcinogenic.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Analysis
topics.groupedBecause: It closes the lecture by summarizing environmental cancer risks and framing exposure choices in terms of risk-benefit trade-offs.
